content: Arbidol is an antiviral medication produced by Masterlek, a pharmaceutical company based in Moscow, Russia. From a chemical perspective, Arbidol is characterized by an indole core structure, which is functionalized at all positions except one with various substituents. Arbidol is considered an alternative to Tamiflu, a drug manufactured by Roche Pharmaceuticals, in the treatment of avian influenza. Its antiviral inhibitory effects are still under investigation, with results ranging from broad acceptance within the pharmaceutical industry to skepticism in some circles. The drug has primarily been studied in Russia and China, where it has demonstrated efficacy against avian influenza. This suggests that Arbidol may serve as a more affordable and cost-effective option compared to the widely used Tamiflu. Preliminary evidence also indicates that Arbidol may be more effective in preventing infections caused by RNA viruses than those caused by DNA viruses. Additionally, it has been explored as a potential treatment for hepatitis C. The mechanism of action of Arbidol includes both immunomodulatory effects and specific antiviral activity against influenza A and B viruses. It works by preventing the interaction between the virus and host cells, as well as inhibiting the penetration of viral particles into cells. This is achieved by blocking the fusion of the viral lipid envelope with cellular membranes. Furthermore, Arbidol induces interferon production, enhances the humoral immune response, and stimulates the phagocytic activity of macrophages. Arbidol is available in tablet and capsule forms, with each dosage containing either 50 mg or 100 mg of the active ingredient, Arbidol®. In terms of pharmacokinetics and usage, side effects in children include sensitization to the drug. No cases of overdose have been reported, and allergic reactions are limited to individuals with hypersensitivity to the medication.
